771.title: Gobind is everything
771.hook: sabh gobind hai: everything is Gobind; there is nothing without Him (Asa, Namdev, ang 485)
771.howItsDone: Namdev's hymn with the refrain sabh gobind hai is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs draw on it to speak of the One present in every heart and all of creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday Namdev sat at the back wall and sang, and the temple turned to face him. Your line was the temple turned. Who did you turn toward? Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Snap the cord of a necklace and you learn something fast. The beads go everywhere: under the couch, into the rug, one rolling off toward the door. While the cord held, you barely noticed it. You were looking at the beads. Namdev, the printer who sang his way into the Guru Granth Sahib, reached for exactly that picture. Yesterday the temple turned toward him. Today he turns the question around: where, in the whole world, is the Lord not? His answer, in the original, is short. Everything is Gobind.
screen: `A SNAPPED NECKLACE.` → `THE CORD YOU NEVER NOTICED.` → `WHERE IS THE LORD NOT?`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 485, and its refrain is sabh gobind hai, sabh gobind hai, gobind bin nahi koi. In paraphrase: everything is Gobind, everything is Gobind; without Gobind there is nothing at all. Gobind is one of the names for the Lord in the Granth. Namdev gives two pictures for it. The first is the necklace. As one thread runs through countless beads, he says in paraphrase, so the Lord runs through everything, warp and weft. The second is water. Waves, foam and bubbles, he says, are not separate from the water. They rise and fall and look like many things, but they're water all the way through. Now the second turn. Namdev admits this isn't obvious. In the same hymn he says the world's dazzling pictures keep people bewildered, and only a rare one understands. That's honest. On plenty of days we see beads, not thread, waves, not water. And the third turn is what he does about it. He says the Guru's teaching woke his mind, and then he invites the listener: look at the Lord's creation, and think it over in your heart. In every heart, within all, there is only the One. Notice the word think. Namdev isn't asking us to pretend the beads aren't there. The colors, the people, the dishes in the sink, all stay. He's asking us to notice the thread through them. Sikhs sing this hymn as gurbani. Its whole teaching fits on one line. Everything is Gobind.
screen: `SABH GOBIND HAI.` · `ONE THREAD THROUGH ALL THE BEADS.` · `WAVES, FOAM, BUBBLES: ALL WATER.` · `ONLY A RARE ONE SEES IT.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IS GOBIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see Him in three things. Sit where you can look around. Let your eyes land on one thing nearby, anything, a cup, a window, your own hand. Rest on it for a few breaths, and say inside, sabh gobind hai. Then a second thing, farther away. Then a third, a sound, or a person, or the air itself. Don't force a feeling. Just let Namdev's line be the thread you run through the three. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Gobind is everything. Namdev's refrain, sabh gobind hai: the one thread through the beads, the water in every wave.
Your line: everything is gobind. Today, when something ordinary catches your eye, a crowd, a meal, a rainstorm, look once for the thread. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: The sultan's demand
772.hook: Namdev sings of a sultan who demanded a miracle, and of the Lord who saved him (Bhairao, Namdev)
772.howItsDone: Namdev's hymn of the sultan is sung as gurbani, and Sikhs often recall it alongside the Gurus' teaching that devotees should not seek to display miraculous powers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thread through the beads and the water in every wave. Your line was everything is gobind. Where did you catch a glimpse of the thread? Day seven hundred seventy-two.

Prove it. Two words that can corner anyone. Show me your God does something, right here, right now, or else. In one of his hymns, Namdev tells of the day a ruler said exactly that to him. Not a friend teasing, but a sultan, with power behind the words, and with Namdev's life on the table. The printer who sang that everything is Gobind is suddenly asked to make Gobind perform. Today: the sultan's demand.
screen: `PROVE IT.` → `A SULTAN, AND A THREAT.` → `MAKE GOBIND PERFORM.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Bhairao, around Ang 1165. In paraphrase, it goes like this. The sultan says: listen, Namdev, let me see the works of your Lord. He has Namdev bound, and a dead cow is set before him. Bring this cow back to life, says the sultan, or I'll cut off your head right here. Now hear Namdev's answer, because it's the heart of the day. How can this be, he says. Nothing happens by my doing. Whatever the Lord does, that is what happens. He won't put on a show. He won't claim a power that isn't his. And he won't drop the Lord to save his neck either. The hymn holds him right there, under threat, honest about what he can and can't do. Then the turn. The hymn says the Lord came to Namdev's side, and the cow rose up, and the sultan, shaken, came asking forgiveness. The hymn tells the rescue quickly. It lingers longer on the moment before it, when Namdev had nothing to offer but the truth. Here's the third turn. Look at where the hymn puts the credit. Not on Namdev. He refused to be the miracle worker the sultan wanted. He stayed a devotee, and the saving came from beyond him. That's why today's line has two halves. Namdev was saved. He was never shown off. Saved, not shown.
screen: `LET ME SEE YOUR LORD'S WORKS.` · `NOTHING HAPPENS BY MY DOING.` · `UNDER THREAT, HE STAYS TRUE.` · `THE CREDIT GOES BEYOND HIM.` · then, large: `SAVED, NOT SHOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay true under pressure. Sit, and let your feet feel the floor. Bring to mind one place in your life where someone wants you to perform. Prove you're right. Prove you're good enough. Say the thing they want to hear. Notice where that pressure sits in your body. Then breathe out slowly, and let one honest sentence form: this is what I can do, and this is what I can't. Rest in that. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you breathe out. The bell holds the time.
The sultan's demand. A ruler orders Namdev to prove his Lord by raising a dead cow, and Namdev says nothing happens by his own doing.
Your line: saved, not shown. Today, when you're pushed to prove yourself, say the honest thing instead of the impressive one. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

773.title: Namdev close
773.hook: a low-caste printer whose songs sit inside the Guru's book, named by a Guru as one who found freedom
773.howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's hymns in kirtan as gurbani, and the Gurus' naming of Namdev and Kabir by their trades is often recalled when Sikhs speak about the rejection of caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sultan's demand: raise the dead cow, or else, and Namdev saying nothing happens by his doing. Your line was saved, not shown. Did you choose the honest thing over the impressive one? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Namaa chheeba. Namdev the printer. That's how a Sikh Guru names him in a hymn, by his trade, the very thing some people of his day held against him. The Guru doesn't hide it or polish it. He says it plainly, and then says what Namdev found. Five days we've spent with this cloth printer: his tools, his cup of milk, the temple at his back, the thread through the beads, the sultan's threat. Today we close his pages by hearing how the Gurus heard him.
screen: `NAMDEV THE PRINTER.` → `NAMED BY HIS TRADE.` → `HOW THE GURUS HEARD HIM.`

segments.voice: The line is in Sri Raag, on Ang 67, in a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. In paraphrase: Namdev the printer and Kabir the weaver found liberation through the perfect Guru. They recognized the Word, and their ego and their caste fell away. Hear what that sentence does. It starts with two working men, named by work that others ranked low. And it ends with freedom. Caste isn't argued with. It just falls away, like a label that no longer has anything to stick to. Now gather Namdev's week into that line. At his printing table, his mind was the measuring yard and his tongue the scissors, and he asked what caste and lineage had to do with the Name. He set down a cup of milk and pleaded until the Lord drank. Thrown out of a temple, he sang at the back wall, and the temple turned. With a string of beads he showed the One thread through everything. And bound before a sultan, he refused to perform and said nothing happens by his doing. Every scene is low to the ground. A workbench, a cup of milk, the back of a building, a prisoner's place. And in each one, the song ends higher than where it began. Sikhs sing his hymns as gurbani, the Guru's word. A printer whose caste was counted low, and whose songs now sit in the Guru's own book. Low caste, high song.
screen: `THE PRINTER AND THE WEAVER.` · `EGO AND CASTE FALL AWAY.` · `A WEEK OF LOW PLACES.` · `HIS SONGS IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · then, large: `LOW CASTE, HIGH SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a humble worker. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose work keeps your day running and who is rarely thanked. The person who cleans the building. The driver. The cook. The one who stocks the shelves at night. Picture their hands at work, the way Namdev's hands worked the cloth. Hold them in your mind with respect for a few breaths. Then decide how you'll honor them today: their name learned, a real thank you, a kindness they didn't expect. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Namdev close. The printer named by his trade in Guru Amar Das's hymn, whose caste fell away and whose songs sit in the Guru's book.
Your line: low caste, high song. Today, learn the name of one person whose work you usually walk past, and use it. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: The shoemaker of Benares
774.hook: Ravidas, a leather-worker whose family were counted low, sings that the leading Brahmins now bow to him (Malar, Ravidas, ang 1293)
774.howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities honor him as a saint whose life challenged caste.

segments.voice: Yesterday was Namdev close: the printer named by his trade in a Guru's hymn. Your line was low caste, high song. Whose name did you learn? Day seven hundred seventy-four.

Some people learn to hide where they come from. They soften the accent, skip the hometown, let others guess. Ravidas did the opposite. Tradition says he worked leather in Benares, the holy city on the Ganges, at a bench where shoes were cut and stitched and mended. Some people of his day wouldn't touch a leather-worker, or drink from the same cup. And yet his hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one of them he tells, without any shame, exactly where he came from. Today: the shoemaker of Benares.
screen: `HIDE WHERE YOU COME FROM?` → `A BENCH IN BENARES.` → `HE SAYS WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Malar, on Ang 1293. Here's its turn, in paraphrase. My people work in leather, and every day they carry dead cattle around Benares. Now the leading Brahmins bow down before me, for I, Ravidas your servant, have taken shelter in your Name. Hear the order of those lines. He starts with the hardest thing to say. Not a soft word for his trade, but the work itself: hauling dead cattle through the lanes of a holy city. Then comes the reversal. The very people who stood at the top of that world now bow to him. And notice what he credits. Not his talent, not his luck. The Name. He has taken shelter there, and that shelter changed how he is seen. Here's the second turn. Ravidas doesn't try to escape his family. He names them first, before he names himself, and keeps them in the song. He holds his people up, dead cattle and all. And the third turn is about the Sikh book. The Granth keeps Ravidas's hymns inside the ragas, under his own name. In gurdwaras his words are sung as gurbani, and Sikhs bow to the book that holds them. A leather-worker's song stands in the same place as a Guru's. He didn't trade his family's name for a grander one. He sang with it. The shoemaker's song.
screen: `MY PEOPLE CARRY DEAD CATTLE.` · `NOW THE BRAHMINS BOW.` · `SHELTER IN THE NAME.` · `SUNG AS THE GURU'S WORD.` · then, large: `THE SHOEMAKER'S SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: polish a pair of shoes. Any pair, yours or someone else's. A cloth, a little polish if you have it, or just a damp rag. Sit with them in your lap. Work slowly, one shoe at a time, around the toe, along the seams, down to the heel. Feel the leather or the canvas under your hand. Think of the hands that cut and stitched them, people whose names you'll never know. If you have no shoes nearby, rub your palms together slowly instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each stroke. The bell holds the time.
The shoemaker of Benares. Ravidas, a leather-worker from a family counted low, who sang that the Brahmins now bow to him, because he took shelter in the Name.
Your line: the shoemaker's song. Today, when you put your shoes on, say to yourself one plain, true thing about where you come from. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

775.title: Begampura, the city without sorrow
775.hook: Ravidas sings of a city without sorrow, tax or fear, where all walk free (Gauri, Ravidas, ang 345)
775.howItsDone: Ravidas's Begampura hymn is sung in gurdwaras as gurbani, and Sikhs and Ravidassia communities often recall it when speaking of a world without caste or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shoemaker of Benares: Ravidas, whose people carried dead cattle, singing that the Brahmins now bowed to him. Your line was the shoemaker's song. Whose work did you honor? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

What would a city look like if nobody in it were afraid? No one dreading the tax collector. No one shut out of a street because of their family. No one first-class and no one second. A leather-worker in Benares, from a family some people kept at the edges, sat down and sang about exactly that city. He even gave it a name. It's in the Guru Granth Sahib, and today we walk through its gate. Begampura.
screen: `A CITY WHERE NO ONE IS AFRAID?` → `A LEATHER-WORKER NAMES IT.` → `THROUGH THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Gauri, on Ang 345. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings: Begampura is the name of the city. There's no sorrow there and no anxiety. No tax, no tribute, no property to worry over. No fear, no wrongdoing, no dread of decline. I've found a home of my own now, brother, where all is well. Notice that the hymn explains its own name. Begampura, the place where sorrow doesn't live. Now look at the list of what's missing. Tax and tribute, the things a powerful man could squeeze out of a poor one. Fear. Ranking. These are weights that press on the poor. Ravidas builds his city by taking them off, one at a time. Here's the second turn. The hymn goes on, in paraphrase: the rule there is steady and lasting; there's no second or third, all are one. The people there wander freely as they please, and no one stops them. Hear that line, nobody stops them, against yesterday's picture of a family carrying dead cattle through the lanes. The free walking is the point. And the third turn. At the close Ravidas signs it as one set free, and says, in paraphrase: whoever is a citizen of that city is my friend. Readers hear Begampura in more than one way. Some hear the soul's home with the Lord, beyond sorrow. Others hear a picture of how a town on earth could be, and some carry this hymn into struggles against caste. The hymn holds both. Begampura is a place where no one is second. The city without sorrow.
screen: `NO SORROW, NO ANXIETY THERE.` · `NO TAX, NO FEAR, NO RANKING.` · `NO SECOND OR THIRD; ALL WALK FREE.` · `THE SOUL'S HOME, OR A TOWN ON EARTH?` · then, large: `THE CITY WITHOUT SORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine your begampura. Close your eyes, or soften them. Let a street come to mind, your own street, or one you know well. Now walk it slowly, the way Ravidas walks his city. Take away one fear the people there carry. Then one wall that keeps someone out. Then one ranking. Let the people move freely, greeting each other. Stay there for a few breaths. Then notice one small thing you could do that would make your real street a little more like it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Begampura. The city Ravidas names and describes in Raag Gauri: no sorrow, no tax, no fear, no second or third, and everyone walking free.
Your line: the city without sorrow. Today, take one weight off one person: a fear eased, a door opened, a ranking ignored. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.title: Sandalwood and castor
776.hook: You are sandalwood and I the poor castor plant beside You, made fragrant by Your nearness (Asa, Ravidas, ang 486)
776.howItsDone: Ravidas's sandalwood hymn is sung in kirtan as gurbani, and Sikhs often use its picture to speak of the sangat, the holy company, whose nearness shapes the one who joins it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Begampura, Ravidas's city with no sorrow, no fear, and no second or third. Your line was the city without sorrow. Whose weight did you lift? Day seven hundred seventy-six.

Sandalwood is prized for its scent, and its fragrance can linger on whatever it touches. The castor plant is a scrappy, weedy shrub that springs up along roadsides and in waste ground. Nobody plants a castor bush for its smell. Yesterday Ravidas built a whole city in song, a place without sorrow. Today he turns from the city to himself, and he reaches for these two plants. He puts them side by side in a hymn, and he knows exactly which one he is. Today: sandalwood and castor.
screen: `SANDALWOOD, PRIZED FOR ITS SCENT.` → `CASTOR, A ROADSIDE WEED.` → `RAVIDAS KNOWS WHICH HE IS.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raag Asa, on Ang 486. In paraphrase, Ravidas sings to the Lord: You are sandalwood, and I am the poor castor plant, living close beside You. From a lowly tree I've become a lofty one, for Your sweet fragrance has come to dwell in me. Hear how the change happens. The castor doesn't turn into sandalwood. It doesn't train or strive its way to a better scent. It just grows near, and the fragrance moves across the gap and settles in. That's the whole picture. Nearness does the work. Here's the second turn. Ravidas keeps going with more pairs. In paraphrase: You are silk, white and yellow, and I am a poor worm. And then the refrain: Madho, I seek the shelter of the company of Your holy ones; I'm full of faults, and You are generous. The company of the holy ones, in Sikh words sangat, is where the nearness happens. It's not only the Lord far above. It's the people you stand beside. A gathering where the Name is sung can rub off on whoever sits in it. And the third turn is about Ravidas himself. This is the leather-worker from two days ago, whose people some refused to touch. In this hymn he doesn't deny that he feels low. He says it plainly. But he doesn't stay there. A low plant beside sandalwood, he says, comes away smelling of something else. Not by changing what it is, but by where it chose to stand. Made fragrant.
screen: `YOU ARE SANDALWOOD, I THE CASTOR.` · `NEARNESS DOES THE WORK.` · `SILK AND A WORM; THE HOLY COMPANY.` · `NOT BY CHANGING, BUT BY STANDING NEAR.` · then, large: `MADE FRAGRANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand near someone good. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one person whose goodness you can almost smell: the kind one, the patient one, the one who leaves a room lighter than they found it. Picture yourself standing beside them for a minute. Don't try to be like them. Just be near, and let something of them settle on you. Then think of one way to spend time near them, or near a gathering like that, this week. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sandalwood and castor. Ravidas's picture: a weedy castor plant growing beside sandalwood, made fragrant by being near.
Your line: made fragrant. Today, choose where you stand: one conversation, one meal, one hour near someone whose goodness rubs off. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

777.title: Who but You
777.hook: who but You would do this, Lord, raising the lowly to honor (Maru, Ravidas, ang 1106)
777.tomorrow: His family carried the dead cattle
777.howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, with the same respect given to the Gurus' own hymns, and this one is often sung as a song of thanks for being raised up.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandalwood and castor: the plain plant growing beside the fragrant tree, made fragrant just by standing close. Who did you stand near, and did any of it rub off? Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

Over a king's head, in the old courts of India, an attendant held a canopy. It said, without a word: this one is honored. Now hold that canopy over someone else. Not a prince. A leather-worker from Benares, the man whose trade made people step aside in the street. That is the picture Ravidas paints in one of his hymns, and he can hardly believe it himself. His question, sung in Raag Maru, is today's word.
screen: `A CANOPY FOR THE KING.` → `HELD OVER A LEATHER-WORKER.` → `WHO BUT YOU?`

segments.voice: The hymn sits on Ang 1106 of the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase, it opens: O Beloved, who but You could do such a thing? Then the Gurmukhi gives a name for God that's worth learning: gareeb nivaaj, the one who cherishes the poor. My Lord, Ravidas sings, places the canopy over my forehead. The royal sign, on him. He doesn't soften what he was in other people's eyes. He says, in paraphrase, that his touch was counted as polluting the world, and on that very person the Lord has poured mercy. Then the line at the hymn's heart: You raise the lowly to the heights, my Gobind, and You fear no one. That last part is quiet but sharp. Lifting a person whom a whole town has agreed to keep low takes nerve. Ravidas's Lord doesn't flinch. And then the hymn opens a door. Ravidas names others who were carried across in the same way: Namdev, Kabir, Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain. This week we've walked with Namdev, the cloth-printer whose milk was drunk and whose temple turned. Kabir we met earlier in this block. Trilochan, Sadhna and Sain are still ahead on this path. Ravidas lines them up like witnesses: it wasn't only me. The hymn closes, in paraphrase: says Ravidas, listen, holy people, the Lord does everything. So the word is a question that isn't really a question. Who but You. It's what someone says when they've been lifted and know they didn't lift themselves.

segments.voice: The practice is to lift one person up. Use the sit to choose who. Let faces come: someone overlooked at work, a relative people talk past, a neighbor nobody greets, a kid who sits at the edge. Stay with one. Then decide one small canopy you could hold over them today: say their name in front of others, ask their opinion first, thank them where it can be heard. Nothing grand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Who but You. Ravidas's question in Raag Maru: who but the cherisher of the poor would hold a king's canopy over a leather-worker's head.

Your line: who but you. This week ran from everything is Gobind to Namdev's sultan to Ravidas's city without sorrow. End it by lifting one person today, and leave the credit where Ravidas left it. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.
